April.
1960. So, what's your name?
Ernest Punch Miller.

And what's your name, Paul? Paul Crawford. Dick Allen is my name. So, we got everybody's name here. All right. Now, I guess I wanted to talk to you about trumpet playing, particularly in the old days. Who were some of the outstanding trumpet players you heard when you were young?

Well, in my time, there was Buddy Petit, Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, Ricard, Louis Armstrong, King Oliver and them. Of course, King Oliver and them were those brothers. King Oliver and Louis Criddy Kepert and them kind of fellas. Another fella by the name of Shatz.
He was older than you or your age?
Who do you mean?
Shatz.
Shatz? No, he's in our class. Yeah.
Who are some of the older ones?
Well, I didn't know nobody but King Oliver and Bunk Johnson. I never met Buddy Bowling.
Edward Clem, did you meet him?
Edward Clem, yeah. I met him too, yeah.
What was he like?
Hmm?
What was he like, Edward Clem?
Oh, you mean in his plane?
Mm-hmm.
Oh, he's one of them good Dixon man men.
Didn't he sound like anybody else in Petit Park?
Well, not to my idea. Him and Joe Howard played something on the order. Mm-hmm. Remember Joe Howard? Yeah, sure. He played on that same order.
Would you describe him as a ratty trumpet player or a straight trumpet player?
No, straight. He was a straight man.
Oh, you got a straight man.
Yeah, that's right. He played a little too. Played with the Robo Show.
What did he play like?
Trumpet.
Now what did he play like? Was he straight or hot or what?
He was just, well he'd get hot, he used to get hot, but he was the first trumpet man. He played straight, but he got hot all right. He got hot.
Did you hear the Robo Show band very much?

Yeah, I used to play at the Lyric Theater. I used to go there all the time. Midnight shows? Before I left. Yeah, they used to have midnight shows. That was before I left New Orleans, way back there. I was here around 22, 23, 24. I started left in 27. Well now, Robo Show, did he feature much jazz at all in his band? About stuff started off like a march, then they, along the middle part of it, they started ragtime and jazz and that's how they played the Overtube, but after that they just played the Showdown.
So he did have some men that could play jazz in his band. Oh yeah, yeah. Would you call him a hot man, Robichaud himself?
No I wouldn't because he was strictly a straight-filing man, you know. He played by ear at all? Yeah, he must have did.

Well let's get down to the actual playing of the trumpet. Well, and what do you mean? Who was what? I mean now, I'm talking about things like breathing and vibrato and the range of different trumpet players, things like that. How do you breathe yourself?
Well, I'd say I breathe about maybe than every other ball.
Really? That often, huh? Yeah. Do you have to? No, you don't have to. I mean, do you have to? No, I don't have to. That's just your style. Yeah.
Yeah. Then I played with a band named Hughie Swift from Chicago, where you played the, if you're playing, you know, brass all together, everybody breathed the same way. Just at the same time.
What about other trumpet players down here? Did any of them feature long phrases, you know, where they would take a breath every four bars, every eight bars, or something like that?

Well, Dick, you got me there. I wouldn't know because we didn't use two trumpets in the same one band here then. Sometime like a tuxedo band, they would use two trumpets sometimes. But the average band we had them days, they said one trumpet, ain't nobody to take breath with you. Just play your own way, you know what I mean? And amateurs for that. I had a bad way of starting off, but I changed. See, I used to play inside of my lip. And then I put the horn on the outside, but then I could catch the notes I wanted, see. But as long as I played in there, I never, I never could make what I wanted. Well, a lot of guys do that, even today. Yeah, they should play just like this. Make a mouthpiece in there. How you do it now? I couldn't do it. How you do it now?
Well, I play it like this now. And that's the standard. Yeah. Now who plays around inside of the lip way today? I see somebody doing that not long ago.

Some of the trumpet players. I forgot who it was though. Seems to me, Kit Howard plays that way now. I believe he does. Maybe Kit Clayton, I can't remember. One of them, yeah, one of them. But you can't get no power like that. You can't put nothing behind it. I wonder why people started that way. I did. I started wrong by not having nobody to share. Of course, when I was in the army, a fellow named Lewis Mathis called him Chiff. He tried to get me away from that, but I, you know, wouldn't listen to him until I got back yet. And I changed, you know. It took me a good while before I could do anything though.
Oh, oh, oh. What are some of the other different ways that guys had of lipping their horns?

Well, Buddy Petit lived way on the side here. On his right side? Right side, yeah. Right side. Right there. Just like that. That's where he played. And if anybody noticed Pop Silistan, he put this part in front, but the bottom part around here. That's what he used to play like. Like that.
Yeah. He'd twist his mouth all around.
Put the mouthpiece on the front and down here on the bottom.
He'd twist his mouth all around.

And we had a fellow here, called himself Young Kid Punch. He fell dead there at Ramport and Tulane Avenue. Going somewhere to play. I was out the lake. And he played like this. Let me see how he played. With his horn pointing up. Oh, just up there. Just a little bit of this.
Turn around to the side a little bit. Now that's about a thirty degree angle up, huh? Mm-hmm. Maybe forty-five, something like that. You never did know his real name like this, yeah?

No. He called himself Kid Punch II. That's what he called himself. I didn't know him that good. He's from over in Algea, I think. And he'd come over here to play a parade or something. And I was like working out at Spanish Food that Sunday, on a Sunday. Boy, that was a worrisome thing to me. Somebody come out there and say, Punch Eight Fell Dave. That was a mess. I kept fooling around there like that, you know. I wonder what's wrong.
Who were you working with at Spanish for? I had my little band there. Kid Punch. How many bands did they have out there in Spanish?

Oh boy, now let me see. I remember the time of the day, there were seven or eight bands out there. No fool from one another's familiar. Back house, one across the street, one on this side of the corner, one over there. You couldn't yield one band for the other.
What were the names of the bands?
Well, René, Beout De Petit, Chris Kelly, maybe Sam Morgan, Sidney Desveen. All them used to play out there.
All of them. And what were some of the places there?

Well, let's call it, like they said, come out to Camp Number 11 or something. There's a big sign up there, you know, when you hit that sign, that walk over the water, you see a sign, they say Camp Number 11. Well, you just go to that one.

Millenburg, yeah, Millenburg.
Not Spanish Four.
Millenburg, that's what I mean, Millenburg. Yeah, them was two different players. Keaton only used to play out Spanish Four.

Some used a hand, but I didn't.

segments.chapter: Opening and New Orleans trumpet players
segments.title: Opening of the interview at Burdett Street
segments.summary: Allen records the date, place and names of those present.

segments.chapter: Opening and New Orleans trumpet players
segments.title: Outstanding trumpet players Punch heard in his youth
segments.summary: Punch names Buddy Petit, Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, Louis Armstrong, King Oliver and others, and which older men he met.

segments.chapter: Opening and New Orleans trumpet players
segments.title: Edward Clem and Joe Howard: straight players who could get hot
segments.summary: Punch describes Edward Clem and Joe Howard as straight trumpet men who could still get hot.

segments.chapter: Opening and New Orleans trumpet players
segments.title: The Robichaux show band at the Lyric Theater
segments.summary: Punch recalls the Lyric midnight shows and how the Robichaux band moved from march to ragtime to jazz.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Breathing and playing inside the lip
segments.summary: Punch breathes every other bar, explains why one trumpet needed no shared breathing, and how he fixed playing inside his lip.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Odd lip positions: Petit, Pop Celestin and Young Kid Punch
segments.summary: Punch demonstrates how Buddy Petit, Celestin and Young Kid Punch placed the horn on the lip.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Young Kid Punch's death and the bands at Spanish Fort and Milneburg
segments.summary: Punch tells of Kid Punch dying on the way to a job while he played at Spanish Fort, and of seven or eight bands there.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Vibrato, flutter tongue, growl and lip trill
segments.summary: Punch and Allen discuss how vibrato, growl and flutter tongue are made, and Punch can no longer growl.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Vibrato and effects among Oliver, Bunk, Kelly, Morgan and Armstrong
segments.summary: Punch says who shook the horn, used a plunger or kept steady, recalls hearing Oliver in Chicago, and describes country trumpeters.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Half valves, glissandos and the third valve
segments.summary: Punch and Allen discuss half-valve effects, glissing up to a note and using the third valve.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: High range of Lenny and rough low playing of Keppard
segments.summary: Punch says Lenny played high like a clarinet but never recorded it well, while Keppard hit notes hard in the staff.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Lionel, Punch's young nephew, gives his name
segments.summary: Allen has Lionel Robinson state his name, age and relation to Punch for the tape.

segments.chapter: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
segments.title: Alternate and false fingering
segments.summary: Allen demonstrates alternate fingering and Punch recalls making notes with the wrong valves.

segments.title: How loud the old trumpeters played
segments.summary: Punch says Armstrong called him one of the loudest in New Orleans, compared with Keppard's strength low down.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's clean round tone and repertoire
segments.summary: Punch praises Buddy Petit's round tone, soft playing and tunes like Maple Leaf Rag and High Society, with a break for stomach trouble.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's diminished chords, ducking notes and second parts
segments.summary: Punch says Petit ran diminished chords, ducked high notes and played a second part under the clarinet.

segments.title: Volume of Chris Kelly, Sam Morgan and Rena
segments.summary: Punch compares the volume of Kelly, Morgan and Rena, blaming Rena's small cup mouthpiece.

segments.title: Truck fire between Dothan and Birmingham
segments.summary: Punch tells how the band's truck caught fire and they lost money, clothes and instruments including a mouthpiece.

segments.title: Deep and shallow cup mouthpieces
segments.summary: Allen asks which mouthpieces players used and Punch says early players used deep cups, later shallow.

segments.title: Joe Smith's deep cup and tone, and his later troubles
segments.summary: Punch praises Joe Smith's lovely tone and deep cup, and he and Allen discuss Joe's drinking and a legal trouble.

segments.title: Custom screw-in mouthpieces and shallow-cup players
segments.summary: Punch lists deep-cup players, explains how custom mouthpieces were fitted, and names shallow-cup players.

segments.title: Mutes: cola bottle, straight mute and Harmon
segments.summary: Punch recalls cola bottle mutes in New Orleans, the buzz mute, and the later Harmon mute he saw in Chicago.

segments.title: Fewer notes in old playing and fast fingering
segments.summary: Punch says old players held notes and later players added many; he is said to be best at fast fingering, with Louis different.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's different phrasing and Guy Kelly's blues
segments.summary: Punch tries to show Louis's unusual figures and says Kelly played pretty blues licks.

segments.title: Third valve and Joe Howard's Satanic Blues
segments.summary: Punch explains using the third valve, says Joe Howard taught him Satanic Blues and plays a sample.

segments.title: Singers in bands and Bob Lyons's band
segments.summary: Punch says musicians rarely sang, credits Louis Dumaine with first singing blues on trumpet, and lists Bob Lyons's men.

segments.title: Playing trumpet behind blues singers
segments.summary: Punch explains filling in when the singer cuts out and notes Johnny Dunn's plunger.

segments.title: Johnny Dunn and Mamie Smith at the Lyric and Midnight Rambles
segments.summary: Punch describes the Lyric's changing weekly shows and the late Midnight Rambles for white patrons.

segments.title: Louis Dumaine behind Chippie Hill on Trouble in Mind
segments.summary: Punch admires Dumaine's chorus before Chippie Hill sings Trouble in Mind and recalls the words.

segments.title: Producing a tone and Jim Horowitz's lip exercises
segments.summary: Punch describes how hard it was to get his low notes and the exercises his teacher gave him.

segments.title: No formal teacher: Chif, Joe Howard and Paul Rozier
segments.summary: Punch says he learned notes from Chif, intonation and fingering from Joe Howard and marching from Paul Rozier.

segments.title: Lionel sings and Clastonet Ward is introduced
segments.summary: Lionel sings I Burned Your Letter and names rock and roll as his favourite; Allen notes Punch's niece.

segments.title: Practice habits and how Punch got into the plantation band
segments.summary: Punch tells of an hour's practice a day and moving from drum to valve trombone, baritone and cornet in the band.

segments.title: A non-musical, churchgoing family
segments.summary: Punch says nobody in his family played and they were church members with no instruments in church.

segments.title: Rehearsing by head: Buddy and Zeb, George Boyd, Eddie Marsh
segments.summary: Punch says bands rarely rehearsed, praises the Petit-Zeb pairing and names his clarinetist George Boyd and Eddie Marsh.

segments.title: Holding a note through a twelve-bar blues chorus
segments.summary: Punch says he could hold a note for a chorus on trumpet, an idea from Joe Howard, unlike clarinetists.

segments.title: Buddy Petit played second voice; no fiddle player
segments.summary: Punch says the trumpet took the lead, Buddy took second voice, and he didn't know Tenette.

segments.title: Buddy Petit at Frenchman's Hall; his looks and stepfather teacher
segments.summary: Punch remembers Petit playing at Francs Amis for light-skinned crowds, his light brown skin, the white callus on his lip and Joe Petit teaching him.

segments.title: Dances of the old days
segments.summary: Punch recalls waltzes and two-steps danced for prizes and the freer dancing afterwards.

segments.title: How Punch and others sat while playing
segments.summary: Punch describes sitting with legs crossed after his operation, stomping his foot, and Ed Marsh playing his horn sideways.

segments.title: Walking in parades and carrying a Mardi Gras parade alone
segments.summary: Punch says fingering made him misstep with the drum and tells of playing a whole parade when the other trumpeter failed to show.

segments.title: Size of a brass band and a bop trumpeter on Sweet Georgia Brown
segments.summary: Punch says brass bands used eight to ten pieces and recalls a young bop player struggling with Sweet Georgia Brown.

segments.title: Where the fingers hit the valves; Lee Collins and Keppard hiding his hand
segments.summary: Punch and Allen compare finger placement, with Lee Collins's unusual overlap and Keppard hiding his hand.

segments.title: Puffing the cheeks: Mutt Carey, Dizzy Gillespie and Louis
segments.summary: Punch says Carey and Gillespie puffed most, Louis some, Petit little, and that he tries to hold in.

segments.title: Learning practical tricks from retired players
segments.summary: Punch and Zango talk about professors versus practical tips, and Punch says retired players share most.

segments.title: Whether white trumpet players played like Black players
segments.summary: Punch says white players at first sounded mechanical but later picked up bending notes and growls from Chicago arrangers.

segments.chapter: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Records with Francois Mosley's band and Mac and Mac in Chicago
segments.summary: Punch lists the personnel on the Francois Mosley record and the pianist on the Mac and Mac session.

segments.chapter: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Johnny Dunn's lack of swing and George Mitchell
segments.summary: Punch says Dunn only played behind singers and could not swing; Allen admires Mitchell's sound.

segments.chapter: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Sunday band battles on the streets of New Orleans
segments.summary: Punch recalls thirty bands on trucks, battles with Sam Morgan, and Buddy Petit's rich tone; winners were judged by hall attendance.

segments.chapter: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Pay for dance jobs
segments.summary: Punch says pay began at two or two and a half dollars a man and reached five dollars when he left.

segments.title: Short bands and a pianist-violinist at the Audubon job
segments.summary: Punch says they did not cut instruments and tells of a man who played piano and violin at a job.

segments.title: Unusual instruments: a piccolo player and balloon blowing
segments.summary: Punch recalls a piccolo player and a dance where he was asked to blow up balloons.

segments.title: Punch's song about old New Orleans dances
segments.summary: Punch sings a song he made up about how the old dances ran and nobody left for a fight.

segments.title: Slide whistle and kazoo players and tub bands
segments.summary: Punch recalls a slide whistler, kazoo players played like trumpets and washboard tub bands.

segments.title: Playing at the Astoria
segments.summary: Punch says he led the first band at the Astoria in 1923-24 and had left Jack Kerr to form his own six-piece band.

segments.title: Working for the Clyde Beatty circus
segments.summary: Punch describes two summers with the Beatty show playing parades and a colored revue, and playing Maryland.

segments.title: Eddie Carl and the Carnes brothers
segments.summary: Punch identifies Eddie Carl, trumpeter, and Eddie and Zinke Carnes, pianists, and the union president Arch Joe.

segments.title: St. Joseph's Night, the Indians and Mardi Gras bands
segments.summary: Punch describes Mardi Gras Indians who clashed with each other, the many bands and the parade routes.

segments.title: Touring with Walter Barnes and bands around Natchez
segments.summary: Punch recounts three years with Walter Barnes, who died in the fire after Punch left, and Bud Scott and Joe Gabriel's string bands.

segments.title: One Sunday with Fate Marable and talk of Foots Thomas
segments.summary: Punch played one Sunday on the boat in place of Louis and discusses Marable's St. Louis men, Foots Thomas and Norman Mason.

segments.title: The spotlight at the Monogram Theater
segments.summary: Punch tells how a spotlight startled him into missing notes during a Sunday solo at the Monogram.

segments.title: The Golden Lily fire
segments.summary: Punch tells of six or eight years at the Golden Lily until a fire, and the owner buying new instruments.

segments.title: The Bookstore job and Junie Cobb's recommendation to Hughie Swift
segments.summary: Punch recounts Tenny Wilson's wife getting him a job at the Bookstore, Junie Cobb hiring him, and a federal raid.

segments.title: Records Punch made with various bandleaders
segments.summary: Punch lists records with Al Wynn, Francois Luzan, Jimmy Wade, Tiny Parham and his own band.

segments.title: The Jelly Roll Morton band and sneaking drinks
segments.summary: Punch tells how he and King Porter hid whiskey in a pot while the bandleader forbade drinking.

segments.title: Jimmy Wade and the Isabella record with Francois Luzan
segments.summary: Punch recalls the Wade band, the Isabella record and drummer Francois's club singing of a greasy pole song.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden's singing and when Punch came to town
segments.summary: Zango mentions Bolden singing; Punch notes he arrived in 1919 after Bolden was gone.

segments.title: I Won't Give You None and Jimmy Bertrand
segments.summary: Allen and Punch try to place the song on the back of Isabella and meeting Bertrand at the Regal.

segments.title: Trying to name a pianist and J.C. Cobb tunes
segments.summary: Allen lists tunes and Punch tries to recall a Chicago pianist he recorded with, unsure if Frisky Foot Jackson.

segments.title: Records with Richard M. Jones and Phil Featheringill
segments.summary: Punch recalls recording blues with Richard M. Jones in the 1930s and being unpaid by Featheringill for four records.
